title: "Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)"
description: "An optimization method that updates model parameters using gradients estimated from individual examples or small batches."
term: "Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)"
letter: "S"

## Simple explanation

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) improves a model by taking repeated
small steps in directions that reduce its loss. Instead of calculating each
step from the entire dataset, it estimates the direction from a sample or
small batch.

## Technical explanation

For parameters $\theta$ and a mini-batch gradient estimate
$\hat{\nabla}L(\theta)$, SGD updates
$\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\hat{\nabla}L(\theta)$, where $\eta$ is the
learning rate. Sampling introduces noise into the estimate, which can
reduce computation per update and affects convergence behavior.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

SGD and its variants train many machine-learning models. Batch size,
learning-rate schedule, data ordering, and optimizer details affect training
stability, speed, generalization, and reproducibility.

## How it works

The training loop samples a mini-batch, computes predictions and loss,
calculates gradients by differentiation, and updates parameters. It repeats
over batches and epochs while monitoring validation metrics and resource
use.

## Practical example

A neural network can train with mini-batches of 32 examples: compute the
batch loss, backpropagate its gradient, and update the weights. A learning
rate that is too high can destabilize training, while one that is too low
can make learning very slow.

## Common misconceptions

- “Stochastic” does not always mean one example at a time; modern SGD
  commonly uses mini-batches.
- SGD does not guarantee finding a global optimum, especially for
  non-convex objectives and finite training budgets.
